ai.definition: Digital Identity Wallets are government-backed applications on smartphones that enable citizens to store, manage and selectively share their digital identities and credentials.
ai.howItWorks: Citizens can issue and receive various types of credentials (e.g., ID cards, driving licenses) through the wallet. These credentials can be shared with third parties in a selective manner without revealing other personal information.
ai.problemSolved: Reduces identity fraud, enhances privacy protection, streamlines government services, and improves cross-border identification processes.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves software development for the wallet application, credential issuance systems, and integration with existing governmental databases. Physical devices (smartphones) are not manufactured but require updates to support the new functionalities.
ai.buildProcess: Developers work on creating a secure environment within the smartphone that can store sensitive data like biometric information or digital signatures. This involves cryptographic protocols for security and privacy.
ai.costDrivers: Costs include software development, testing, implementation of security measures, integration with existing systems, and ongoing maintenance. Initial setup costs are high due to the complexity and need for robust cybersecurity infrastructure.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to grow as more governments adopt it, but widespread adoption faces challenges such as privacy concerns and interoperability issues between different systems.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by country; some are supportive of digital identity initiatives while others may have strict data protection laws that could hinder implementation. Interoperability standards need to be established for cross-border use.
ai.risks: Cybersecurity threats, privacy concerns, and the risk of technological obsolescence as new technologies emerge. There's also a risk of regulatory pushback or lack of support from certain governments.
ai.profitability: Initial costs are high but could lead to cost savings in long term through reduced fraud and streamlined government services. Revenue models may include transaction fees for third-party access to credentials, but this is not yet well established.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments might focus on enhancing security features, expanding the range of credentials that can be stored, improving user interface, and developing standards for cross-border interoperability.

glossary.def: The process of creating and distributing digital documents or badges to individuals.
A method where a user can choose which parts of their identity information are shared with third parties, maintaining privacy while providing necessary verification.

subsystems.name: Wallet app
subsystems.role: runs on the user's phone, stores credentials securely and presents them when requested.

subsystems.name: Issuer systems
subsystems.role: government agencies and trusted organisations create and sign digital credentials.

subsystems.name: Verifiable credential standards
subsystems.role: define how credentials are structured, signed, and presented with selective disclosure.

subsystems.name: Trust and revocation infrastructure
subsystems.role: lets verifiers confirm that an issuer is authorised and that a credential is still valid.

subsystems.name: Verifier software
subsystems.role: requests credentials from wallets and checks them against policy.

buildSteps.title: Establish legal and technical framework
buildSteps.detail: Governments pass laws recognising digital identity and adopt open standards for wallets, credentials and trust.

buildSteps.title: Build issuer infrastructure
buildSteps.detail: Agencies and trusted bodies integrate identity proofing, credential signing and issuance APIs.

buildSteps.title: Develop the wallet app
buildSteps.detail: A mobile app is built with secure storage, a clear consent interface and support for multiple credentials.

buildSteps.title: Implement selective disclosure
buildSteps.detail: Cryptographic schemes such as SD-JWT or BBS+ are integrated so a holder can reveal single attributes without exposing the whole credential.

buildSteps.title: Set up trust registries
buildSteps.detail: Lists of authorised issuers and verifiers are published, along with status lists for revocation.

buildSteps.title: Pilot with real users
buildSteps.detail: Large-scale pilots test usability, security and interoperability across public and private services.

buildSteps.title: Roll out nationally
buildSteps.detail: Wallets are offered to all citizens and accepted for government services, age checks and financial onboarding.

buildSteps.title: Enable cross-border recognition
buildSteps.detail: Standards and trust frameworks are aligned so wallets are accepted in other countries.

prerequisites.why: wallet keys and credentials need a hardware-backed keystore to resist extraction.
schemes like SD-JWT and BBS+ are standardised but not yet widely deployed at scale.
OpenID for Verifiable Credentials and W3C standards exist, but adoption across vendors is still maturing.
regulations such as the EU's eIDAS 2.0 require wallets, but many countries lack equivalent frameworks.
trust registries and status lists are being piloted but are not yet universal.

pathway.milestone: national and EU large-scale pilots test wallets for e-government and age verification
pathway.unlocks: real-world evidence on usability, security and privacy.

pathway.milestone: first production rollouts under regulations like eIDAS 2.0
pathway.unlocks: citizens can use a government-backed wallet for public services.
a wallet works for banks, airlines and online platforms across borders.

pathway.milestone: ubiquitous adoption with advanced privacy features such as zero-knowledge proofs
pathway.unlocks: minimal disclosure becomes the default for proving identity online and offline.
